query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In dual‐phase stainless steels used for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, the high corrosion resistance is primarily due to the rapid formation and maintenance of a chromium‐rich passive oxide film. This film develops because microstructural features (such as high grain boundary and phase interface densities) promote accelerated Cr diffusion to the surface while less noble elements (e.g., Fe) selectively dissolve.
generation.material_initial_state: Dual‐phase stainless steel (e.g., DS2205) in its standard, coarse‐grained condition with conventional alloying levels (sufficient Cr content).
generation.intervention: Modify the microstructure by subjecting a set of identical steel samples to severe plastic deformation (or other grain-refining techniques) to produce an ultrafine-grained structure that increases grain boundary density without altering the overall alloy chemistry.
generation.conditions: Expose both the modified (fine-grained) and unmodified (coarse-grained) steels to controlled corrosive environments representative of real-world conditions: aqueous media such as 0.6 M NaCl solution for chemical processing, and high-temperature molten salts (e.g., NaCl-KCl-MgCl2) for nuclear-power applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced density of grain boundaries and phase interfaces that facilitate rapid Cr diffusion to the surface, thereby leading to a self-healing, continuous, chromium-enriched passive oxide film.
generation.mechanism: Under corrosive conditions, the less noble elements (primarily Fe) dissolve preferentially. The resulting local chemical potential gradient, aided by abundant grain boundaries, drives Cr from the bulk to the surface where it oxidizes, forming a protective film that slows further corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Steel samples with a refined, ultrafine-grained structure are expected to exhibit a thicker, more uniform, and stable Cr-rich oxide film, resulting in significantly lower corrosion rates compared to coarse-grained steels under identical conditions.
generation.baseline: Conventional coarse-grained dual-phase stainless steels with standard alloy composition and typical passivation behavior.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to be valid when the steel maintains a minimum Cr level necessary for passivation and within operational conditions (temperatures, salt compositions, and stress states) typical of chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments. Extreme variations in these conditions or radical composition changes may alter the mechanism.
generation.uncertainty: The extent to which grain boundary density versus selective dissolution controls film formation remains uncertain, as do the quantitative effects of radiation-induced microstructural changes in nuclear environments.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of otherwise identical dual-phase stainless steel samples: one set processed to achieve an ultrafine-grained microstructure (increased grain boundary density) through severe plastic deformation, and a control set with the original coarse-grained structure. Expose both sets to a corrosive aqueous environment (e.g., 0.6 M NaCl at an elevated temperature) and a high-temperature molten salt environment under identical conditions. Use surface characterization tools (XPS, SEM) to analyze the Cr-rich passive film development and measure corrosion rates via electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and mass loss analysis over time.
measurements: Corrosion rate (mass loss, current density measurements)
Cr oxide film thickness, uniformity, and composition (via XPS and SEM)
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to gauge film protectiveness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ultrafine-grained samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in the formation and maintenance of a thicker, more uniform Cr-rich passive film, and if their corrosion rates are comparable to or higher than those of the coarse-grained controls under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Severe plastic deformation (SPD) techniques enable the fabrication of ultrafine-grained (UFG) or nanocrystalline (NC) materials in bulk forms suitable for load-carrying structural applications []. With the advent of SPD, there has been an increasing demand to clarify the effect of UFG/NC formation on corrosion from a practical viewpoint, especially with regard to the classic topic of the effect of grain size on corrosion [,]. Among the various materials investigated to date, stainless steels exhibited mostly improved corrosion resistance by forming UFG structures by SPD [,,,,,,,]. The enhanced corrosion resistance of UFG/NC SSs compared with coarse-grained (CG) materials has been mostly attributed to greater Cr enrichment in the passivation film [,,,,,,,,], which has been validated experimentally by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) [] and recently by Cs-corrected scanning-transmission electron microscopy (STEM) [,]. Two possibilities for the enhanced Cr enrichment in the passivation film of UFG/NC materials have been proposed. cited_evidence.kind: web:4.1. Effect of Alloy Composition on Molten Salt Corrosion Behavior
cited_evidence.text: Cr depletion depth increased significantly in DS2205 compared to AlCoCrFeNi2.1, with an increase in temperature from 450 °C to 650 °C. At 650 °C, the Cr depletion depth for AlCoCrFeNi2.1 was ~50 μm, while that for DS2205 was ~300 μm. This suggests that Al in the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 acted as a sacrificial element and reduced Cr dissolution rate in the molten salt compared to DS2205. Redox control technique has been utilized for corrosion mitigation in molten fluoride and chloride salts []. Dissolution of Al and Cr into the molten salt resulted in the formation of AlCl3 and CrCl2, which formed a redox couple of Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2. At the redox potential, Co, Ni, and Fe become relatively nobler and their dissolution is thermodynamically unfavorable. These findings suggest that Al/AlCl3 and Cr/CrCl2 couple may be used as redox buffer to slow or stop the dissolution of Fe, Co, and Ni from AlCoCrFeNi2.1 [].
